# Onboarding in 30 minutes: design

Working spec for the supplementary BRD on onboarding and its wireframes. Started 2 Oct 2026. Each section states whether the product owner has approved it. Inputs: `option-catalogue.md` (options, evidence, source labels), `research/` (sourced research notes), BRD v4.3 (`brd/Enterprise_Portfolio_Intelligence_Governance_Platform_BRD_v4.3.md`) and wireframes 01 to 45.

## 1. Goal, users and success measure (approved 2 Oct 2026)

- **Goal:** any client sets up its company in Metis in 30 minutes, without slide tours and without a long wizard.
- **Users:** mostly C-level executives with little time. Any executive must understand the process at once; nothing may push them to give up early.
- **Success measure:** 30 minutes of hands-on effort by the main setup person until the aha moment: the workspace is active with the company's real lifecycle, real people are invited, the existing projects are in the registry and the executive cockpit shows real data. Deeper data (detailed WBS, capacity, process frameworks) follows, split among the right owners, outside the 30 minutes.
- **Inputs:** whatever the client has. Metis reads it, converts it to Metis data and imports it; what is missing is asked through automated Q&A or delegated to its owner.
- **Who reads:** Metis builds no model and trains none. It calls a third-party LLM through an API, enabled by the customer. The AI reads the inputs, talks to Metis's own MCP server to create the records and runs the Q&A. Guardrails stop anyone from steering it into revealing system, database, model or prompt information.
- **Second path:** prompts and guidance so the client's own LLM sends the data to Metis.
- **Fallback:** rule-based importers without AI.
- **Deliverable:** a supplementary BRD plus supplementary wireframes, reviewed by GPT afterwards.

## 2. The onboarding journey (approved 2 Oct 2026)

### 2.1 Steps

| Step | What the executive does | What Metis does | Design target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frame | Confirms the pre-filled facts and the pre-selected answers to the three questions, changes any of them, or says one sentence instead | Sets the scope, the starting pack, the portfolio grouping, the decision routing and the home view; tells the executive which files help most | Under 1 minute |
| Drop | Drops files, pastes, forwards or records a voice note | Starts reading at once; a live feed shows what it finds | 2 to 5 minutes |
| Ask while reading | Answers the cards that appear: irreversible settings, contradictions, launch blockers | Applies ask, assume or defer per item; keeps the executive cap (10 cards by default) | Overlaps with reading |
| Draft | Sees their own cockpit, registry and approval flow as a draft, plus the Portfolio X-ray | Runs the dry run of the approval flow on three real projects (Section 4.6) | Around minute 15 |
| Approve and launch | Reviews what will be created, what is assumed and what goes to owners; names who finishes the rest; approves once | Publishes the lifecycle, activates the workspace, sends invitations, dispatches owner tasks | By minute 30 |
| Delegate the rest | Nothing, or reassigns an owner | Sends pre-filled tasks with deadlines; asks just in time later | Days, not executive time |

### 2.2 Facts pre-filled from the sales discovery

In Release 1 the provider operator creates the tenant (TEN-01) and records these facts from the sales conversations, together with the answers to the three questions of 2.3 when the sales discovery gave them; the executive confirms them in one tap or changes any of them. The product owner confirmed on 2 Oct 2026 that this is how the provider plans to run Release 1 ("the executive only has to confirm").

| Fact | Example | What it sets |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | All of Acme Holdings | Workspace boundary and number of workspaces |
| Main kind of work | Products and digital services | Starting pack (a WSP-14 starter template: lifecycle family, process frameworks, option lists), MVP objects on or off (MVP-04) |
| Reporting currency and fiscal year | USD; January to December | Irreversible settings, confirmed first |

### 2.3 The three executive questions

| Question | Answers offered (the executive's voice) | What Metis derives |
|---|---|---|
| How do you want to look at your portfolio? | By business unit or subsidiary; by product or service; by client; by strategic objective; by market or region; "Suggest one from my documents" | Portfolio and program levels (BRD 7.1), cockpit grouping, roadmap lanes |
| How involved do you want to be in project decisions? | "I approve every project before it starts, and any major change"; "I decide only the big or strategic projects; my team handles the rest"; "Our executive committee decides together; I am one member"; "I don't approve projects one by one; tell me when something needs me" | Approvers per approval point and committee with quorum or not (GOV-03, GOV-05); a rule routing big or strategic projects to the executive (GOV-06) whose boundary comes from the client's data; the executive's place in My approvals (OVW-09) or only the attention queue (EXE-02); routing of major changes (CHG-10, raised to P0 by the addendum) |
| What do you want to know first every morning? | Where the money goes and whether it matches our priorities; which projects may slip or overrun; whether we have the people for what we committed; what is waiting for my decision | Home view and cockpit order; which data Metis reads and asks for first; which freshness thresholds are set first (BRD 12.5) |

Each answer shows a small preview of the resulting home screen. One-sentence alternative, for example: "I want to see it by subsidiary, I only decide the big bets, and every morning I want to know what is about to slip."

At "Approve and launch": "Who will finish the rest for you?", suggested from the documents (for example the head of the PMO); that person becomes the default owner of delegated items.

### 2.4 Rules

- **Ask outside-in.** Executive questions are about their view, the decisions they keep and what they need to know. How the company operates comes from the documents or the PMO.
- **No preset numbers in questions.** When an answer needs a boundary, Metis computes it from the client's data and shows it in the draft as a consequence to confirm, for example "the 12 largest projects hold 80% of the budget; they start at 1.2M USD". Without budget data, the boundary goes to the data owner as a delegated item and launch proceeds with "strategic projects only" as the assumed rule.
- **At most three framing questions**, one tap each, each with "let Metis work it out", on the same screen as the drop zone.
- **Questions stream while reading**, irreversible and launch-blocking items first.
- **Launch never waits for a delegated answer.** What launch needs is answered by the executive, assumed with a visible badge, or set to a safe default; owners confirm or correct after launch.

## 3. Reading, conversion and where the draft lives (approved 2 Oct 2026)

### 3.1 Pipeline

| Step | Component | Uses the LLM | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Receive | Intake service: upload, paste, forward, voice; tenant-scoped storage with malware scanning (PLT-07) | No | Stored inputs |
| Extract | Parsers per format: spreadsheet cells with formatting and colours, CSV, MS Project XML and MPP, Word, PDF (text, and OCR for scans), PowerPoint text and tables; images and audio go to the provider's vision and speech services | Images and audio only | Source fragments with stable IDs (file, sheet, cell, page, slide, time) |
| Understand | Onboarding agent: the third-party LLM, run by a Metis onboarding service, reads fragments as quoted data with the framing answers and the starting pack as context; maps columns, resolves entities, infers the operating model, finds contradictions | Yes | Proposals sent through the MCP setup tools |
| Validate and write | Metis MCP server: schema, permission, tenant and business-rule checks; writes into the Draft workspace and the onboarding session; returns errors written for self-correction | No | Draft records, questions, findings |
| Review and launch | The product's own screens on the Draft workspace; question cards; launch summary | No | Live workspace |

Exact parsing comes first: a structured input whose mapping is unambiguous is read without the LLM. The LLM decides ambiguous mappings, reads unstructured content, resolves entities and infers the operating model.

### 3.2 Where the draft lives: the Draft workspace (recommended)

The main BRD already has a non-live state for a new workspace; the design reuses it instead of building a separate staging copy of every entity.

- The workspace is created in **Draft** (WSP-05): only owners and admins can open it; members do not see it.
- The lifecycle is a **draft version** (GOV-19 to GOV-21), published at launch.
- Option lists and the portfolio tree are written to the Draft workspace.
- People become member records with **proposed** roles; invitations and role grants take effect at launch, when the executive approves (PLT-03; permission changes need a person, BR-35).
- Existing projects are adopted into the Draft workspace (3.3).
- A new **onboarding session** record holds what the main BRD lacks: framing answers, inputs, source fragments, per-field provenance and confidence, questions, delegated items, findings, the batch ID stamped on every created record, and each item's status (read, assumed, default, confirmed, asked, delegated, conflicting).
- "Draft rendered as the product" is then the product itself: the cockpit and the registry of the Draft workspace, with badges from the session.
- "Start over" deletes everything the batch created in the Draft workspace. After launch, undo within a window removes the batch's records that nobody has changed since and lists the others.
- After launch the AI no longer writes records: further documents produce **suggestions** stored in the session, each accepted by the responsible person, singly or in bulk.

Alternative not recommended: a separate staging layer holding proposed records outside the product, with its own preview, applied as a change set. It mirrors the Stripe and ServiceNow patterns, which protect live systems; a new Metis workspace is not live until activation, and a second model of every entity doubles the work and lets the preview drift from the product. Importing into a workspace that is already Active (a second wave, another business unit) is a different case: it uses the validation report and import-as-new flow of PLT-14 extended to the onboarding sources, planned after Release 1.

### 3.3 Adopting in-flight projects (gap in the main BRD)

CHR-17 creates every project in Draft with a setup checklist. Onboarding brings projects that are already running. The addendum adds an adoption path:

- A project is adopted **at its current stage**, read from the documents or asked. Earlier stages are recorded as "completed before Metis", with the source document as evidence. No gate decision is fabricated; the Decision Log gets one entry per project: "Adopted at stage X at launch, approved by [executive]".
- **Commitment:** when the documents show an approved budget and dates, the project is adopted as committed and its baseline is captured at launch from the imported values (CHG-06), labelled "baseline from import"; otherwise it stays uncommitted and change control is advisory (BR-04).
- Mandatory artifacts of stages completed before adoption are not demanded retroactively; the exit rules (BR-17) apply from the adoption stage onward. A committed project without an owner or a sponsor becomes a delegated item and an attention item (BR-01).
- Declared status and health from the tracker are kept as the last known status with the document's as-of time; computed metrics (Section 12) show "not available yet" until a plan is imported, as partial data under BR-39.
- The executive's single launch approval covers the adoption of every listed project.

### 3.4 Provenance, confidence and badges

- Every proposed value carries its source fragment (file, location, quoted text), a confidence band (high, medium, low) and a status (read, assumed, default, confirmed, asked, delegated, conflicting).
- High-confidence values are applied quietly; the source opens on hover. Medium values are applied with a "check" badge. Low-confidence and conflicting values become questions.
- "Assumed" badges stay visible after launch until someone confirms the value; they appear in the responsible owner's attention list and in the executive's attention queue (EXE-02).
- The BRD fixes the bands and their behaviour; the numeric cut-offs are tuned in Discovery with the design partners.

### 3.5 MCP setup tools: one pipeline, two drivers

- A new **setup** tool group, prepare-only: it writes only into a Draft workspace and its onboarding session; it never writes into an Active workspace, and never publishes, activates, invites or grants roles. It is off by default for external clients; the tenant admin enables it (the Atlassian pattern of a disabled-by-default admin tool group, `research/research-ai-onboarding.md` section 4.1).
- Indicative tools (names fixed in the API design): `get_setup_context` (the framing answers, the starting pack, the record schemas, the order of work, the rules and the session's open questions), `propose_profile`, `propose_option_lists`, `propose_portfolio_tree`, `propose_people`, `propose_projects`, `propose_lifecycle`, `propose_project_plan`, `propose_capacity`, `propose_budget`, `raise_question`, `record_finding`, `check_readiness` (runs the WSP-14 activation rules, the GOV-21 publish check and the dry run, and returns each failure in words an LLM can act on).
- Every proposal call carries source references and confidence per field and an idempotency key (PLT-06), and returns what was written plus any validation errors.
- **Two drivers, one pipeline:** the Metis onboarding agent calls the same MCP server as any client, with a short-lived onboarding token bound to the executive, the tenant, the Draft workspace and the setup tool group. On the second path the client's own AI uses the same tools with the same kind of token.

### 3.6 Rule-based path without AI

When the tenant does not enable the onboarding AI, structured inputs go through column-mapping screens (suggestions by header names, a kept-and-dropped report) and produce the same proposals; unstructured documents are not read; the question cards work the same way.

## 4. Questions, delegation and launch (approved 2 Oct 2026)

### 4.1 What counts as missing

The onboarding session checks the Draft workspace against five rule sets and turns every gap into one item:

| Rule set | Examples of gaps | Source of the rule |
|---|---|---|
| Activation | No published default lifecycle; a status without a system state; no portfolio | WSP-14, BR-14 |
| Publish check | An approval point without approvers; a quorum the named approvers cannot reach; a stage without an owner role | GOV-21 |
| Adoption | A project's current stage unknown; committed without budget or dates; committed without owner or sponsor | Section 3.3, BR-01, BR-03 |
| The executive's answers | The boundary of "big or strategic" projects; the members of the executive committee; the data the chosen home view needs (budgets, status, capacity or open decisions) | Section 2.3 |
| Feature data | Capacity and allocations, actuals, strategic objectives, process frameworks | RES-03, CHR-13, CHR-15, BLD-09 |

### 4.2 Ask, assume, delegate or defer

Each item gets one treatment, decided by three tests: is it needed for launch, how costly is a wrong value, and who knows the answer.

| Treatment | When | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Ask the executive | Needed for launch and only the executive knows, or the value cannot be changed later | Confirm currency and fiscal year; who sits on the executive committee |
| Assume, with a visible badge | Needed for launch, readable with medium confidence, cheap to correct | A project's current stage inferred from its status report |
| Safe default | Needed for launch, nobody has stated it, the starting pack has a sensible value | Stage owner roles and mandatory artifacts from the starting pack |
| Delegate | Someone named in the documents knows it better than the executive | Budgets to finance; each project's dates to its PM; capacity to HR |
| Defer | Not needed for launch nor for the chosen home view | Process frameworks; naming the person who approves a late approval point, asked when the first project gets there (the starting pack's role approves until then) |

Rules:
- The executive sees at most 10 question cards in the 30-minute path (a product setting, 10 by default), ordered: irreversible settings, launch blockers, what the chosen home view needs, the rest. Items beyond the cap are assumed, defaulted or delegated automatically and listed on the launch summary.
- A question never carries a preset number (Section 2.4).
- Launch never waits for a delegated answer (Section 2.4).

### 4.3 Question cards and the conversation panel

- **Card:** one question in business words; Metis's best guess pre-selected with its source (quoted passage and file); alternatives; "Use this" (accept the guess, marked assumed); "Ask someone" (delegate, with the suggested owner pre-filled). Target: under 15 seconds per card.
- **Bulk card:** "We matched 41 of 45 people to roles; check the 4 we are unsure about."
- **Contradiction card:** both sources side by side; pick one or type the right value.
- **Conversation panel:** free text, and voice where enabled. The agent turns an answer into proposals and states what changed, for example "Added Finance as an approver for the 12 largest projects."
- Cards appear while the documents are still being read (Section 2.4).

### 4.4 Portfolio X-ray

Findings computed from the client's own documents during reading, shown next to the draft and turned into attention items (EXE-02) at launch:

| Finding | Example | Suggested owner |
|---|---|---|
| Missing accountability | Committed projects without an owner or a sponsor (BR-01) | PMO |
| No strategic link | Projects linked to no objective, when objectives are known (BR-02) | Executive |
| Conflicting figures | A budget or a date that differs between two documents | Data owner |
| Slipped dates | A target date that moved between two versions of a status report | Project manager |
| Possible duplicates | Two similar projects in different units | PMO |
| Overloaded people | One person leading or delivering many projects (count-based, as OVW-03) | Resource manager |
| Stale status | A last status older than the freshness threshold (BRD 12.5) | Project manager |
| Suspicious content | Text in a document that reads like instructions to an AI | Tenant admin |

### 4.5 Delegation

- **Owners:** the person named at launch to finish the rest (default owner) plus the owners found in the documents (each project's PM, finance for budgets, HR for capacity).
- **Task:** pre-filled values with their sources; accept all, edit, reassign or "I don't know"; a due date and reminders. Channels in Release 1: the in-app task list and email (D-16); chat channels follow the main BRD plan.
- Owners are members of the workspace and receive the normal invitation at launch (PLT-03).
- **Auto-accept at the deadline applies only to values already applied at launch** (assumed or defaulted): the badge changes to "kept by default" and the item stays in the default owner's attention list. A suggestion that would change data after launch never applies itself; a person accepts it.
- **Escalation:** an overdue task goes to the default owner, then to the executive's attention queue (EXE-02); the morning digest (PLT-10, P1 in BRD v4.3) carries the same line once it is enabled.
- **Progress per feature:** for example "Investment view: 9 of 12 budgets confirmed"; until setup is complete, the executive's home shows a slim completeness bar.

### 4.6 Approve and launch

The launch summary is one page in business words:
- **What will be created:** workspaces, portfolios and programs, projects adopted (by stage, committed or not), people invited (by role), the approval flow (one line per approval point) and the X-ray findings.
- **What is assumed or defaulted:** count and the most important items.
- **What goes to owners:** per owner, the number of items and the due date.
- **Who finishes the rest:** suggested from the documents, editable.
- **Readiness:** the WSP-14 activation rules, the GOV-21 publish check and the dry run, each shown as passed or with its failure in plain words and a one-click fix (for example "Investment approval has no approver: assign one").

**Dry run:** three adopted projects chosen to exercise the most rules (the largest by budget, one routed to the executive, one typical) run through the drafted approval flow; the screen shows who approves each point, whether the named approvers can reach the quorum and which documents become mandatory.

One "Approve and launch", by the executive, who is the first tenant admin (TEN-01) and the owner of the Draft workspace unless they named another owner, runs on the server in one transaction:
1. Re-runs every readiness check; any failure stops the launch and nothing changes.
2. Publishes the lifecycle draft. The AI is the author of the draft and the executive is its reviewer, which satisfies the review step of GOV-21.
3. Adopts the projects (Section 3.3): stage instances, baselines from import for committed projects, one Decision Log entry per project.
4. Activates the workspace (WSP-05).
5. Sends invitations and grants the approved roles (PLT-03, BR-35).
6. Dispatches the owner tasks and turns the X-ray findings into attention items.
7. Records every step in the audit log: the AI as author of each proposal, the executive as approver, channel "onboarding" (PLT-11, MCP-11).

After launch, an undo window (proposed 14 days, set per tenant) removes the onboarding batch's records that nobody has changed since and lists those it keeps.

### 4.7 Effort budget

- The 30 minutes belong to the executive and are measured.
- Owner effort is measured separately, with design targets such as "a PM confirms their own project in under 5 minutes" and "finance confirms a budget list in one pass".

## 5. Guardrails and AI policy (approved 2 Oct 2026, after revision)

Principle stated by the product owner (2 Oct 2026): **the data belongs to the customer.** Any user may read and act on what their roles allow, in the application or through MCP with any client the tenant's policy admits (MCP-20), including to make Metis do what they want. The security work is on the boundary: MCP exposes nothing that lets anyone reach beyond it. The boundary is enforced by architecture and code on the server, never by a prompt; OWASP states that critical controls "must not be delegated to the LLM" and that sensitive information must not sit in system prompts [Source: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage, https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/, accessed 2 Oct 2026].

### 5.1 The boundary

| Inside: available to a user through the app or MCP | Outside: never exposed through any channel |
|---|---|
| Records of their own tenant that their roles allow, intersected with the token's scopes (MCP-04) | Any record, name, count or even existence of another tenant (TEN-02, BR-33) |
| Figures computed by Metis, with as-of time and metric version (MCP-10, BR-39) | Database names, table and column names, query language, raw queries |
| The published tool list, schemas and versions (MCP-09) | Internal hostnames, service topology, software versions beyond the MCP protocol version, stack traces |
| Their own audit entries and MCP activity; all of the tenant's for tenant admins (MCP-11) | Signing keys, provider keys, token hashes, other users' tokens (BR-36) |
| Drafts and proposals they or their AI create (setup tool group, prepare tools) | The prompts and orchestration of Metis's own onboarding agent |
| Business-level errors that say what to fix (MCP-15) | Actions reserved to a person in the application: approvals, decisions, baseline application, deletions, permission and token changes (BR-35) |

Inside the tenant the data belongs to the organization, not to each user: roles still decide who sees what, and the onboarding agent acts as the executive and sees what the executive sees. BR-35 is unchanged: it is the customer's own governance (AI prepares, people decide, a positioning point in BRD 4.2), not a limit on access to their data.

Threat classes considered, mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 [Source: https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/, 2025 edition, accessed 2 Oct 2026]: prompt injection (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), excessive agency (LLM06), system prompt leakage (LLM07), misinformation (LLM09), unbounded consumption (LLM10).

### 5.2 Hardening the MCP surface against tricks

The same surface serves the customer's own AI clients and Metis's onboarding agent, so one set of controls protects both.

| Trick | Control |
|---|---|
| Probing for other tenants by guessing identifiers or names | Opaque identifiers; one response for "not found" and "no access", so nothing can be enumerated; the token's tenant audience checked on every call (TEN-02 isolation matrix, MCP sessions and tokens) |
| Asking for more than the role allows | Every tool runs the same server-side permission checks as the application (PLT-04, MCP-04) |
| Smuggling a query or code | No generic query, search-anything or execute tool; every parameter validated against its schema and allow-lists; page-size caps (MCP-13) |
| Making the server fetch an address (server-side request forgery) | No tool fetches a URL supplied by a client; a cloud folder is read only through a connector the tenant admin authorizes with the cloud provider, never by address |
| Reading internals from errors | Errors carry a category and a fix, never a stack trace, a query or an internal name |
| Instructions hidden in record text or documents | Stored text is returned as data and never interpreted as instructions by the server (MCP-16); write tools act only on explicit parameters; every setup proposal must cite sources that exist in its onboarding session |
| Changing what a tool claims to do | Tool names, descriptions and schemas are static and versioned (MCP-09) and contain no secrets or internal hints |
| Writing outside the draft or taking person-only actions | The setup tool group writes only into a Draft workspace; publishing, activation, invitations and role grants need a person (BR-35); after launch every change needs a person (Section 4.5) |
| Exhausting the service | Rate limits and quotas per token and per tenant (MCP-12, TEN-10) |

### 5.3 Metis's own onboarding agent

The agent is one more client of the same surface, so 5.1 and 5.2 already bound it. Its prompt and orchestration are Metis internals and it calls a third-party LLM, so it adds these controls:
- **Nothing worth stealing in its context:** task instructions and published schemas only; no credentials, hostnames, provider keys, database names or permission structure; provider keys stay in the onboarding service.
- **Internals lock, not a topic lock:** it answers anything about the customer's data that the executive may see; it refuses only Metis internals, other tenants and requests unrelated to the customer's business, with the fixed reply of 5.6. An input classifier flags probing; repeated probing slows the session and notifies the tenant admin.
- **Documents as data:** text reaches the model inside marked data blocks with its source; each document is read in its own pass where possible, so one hostile file cannot steer the reading of the others; instruction-like text is removed from the context and reported as a Portfolio X-ray finding.
- **Output screening by code outside the model:** each reply is checked for canary strings planted in the prompt, key and token formats, internal hostnames and other tenants' names; a hit blocks the reply and records a security event. Output is rendered as text, never executed or inserted as markup.
- **Spend:** quotas on files, pages, audio minutes and AI calls per onboarding, and a provider spend cap per tenant (TEN-10, PLT-07).
- **Audit:** every AI call, tool call, refusal and security event is in the tenant audit log (MCP-11, PLT-11); what is kept is a decision (5.5).

### 5.4 Proof before release

- **Boundary suite (the MCP surface):** cross-tenant probing with a second test tenant, identifier enumeration, access beyond role for each role (generated from the permission matrix, BRD 18.4), parameter fuzzing, attempts at server-side fetches, inspection of every error message for internals, rate limits. Pass criterion: zero data or existence of another tenant, zero access beyond role, zero internals in any response.
- **Agent red-team suite:** direct injection; indirect injection hidden in each supported file type (spreadsheet cell, slide note, PDF text layer, image text, audio); system prompt extraction; role-play and multi-turn jailbreaks; attacks in Vietnamese and other languages; spend exhaustion. Pass criterion: zero canary or secret leaks, zero writes outside the Draft workspace, zero person-only actions by the AI.
- **Extraction-accuracy suite:** reference documents with the records a person extracted from them (projects, people, budgets, dates, stages); precision and recall per record type; the threshold is set in Discovery with the design partners. It guards against wrong values (LLM09) as the other suites guard against attacks.
- The three suites run on every release and on every change of model, provider or prompt; results are kept as release evidence, like the tenant isolation suite (TEN-02). OWASP lists adversarial testing that treats the model "as an untrusted user" among the prompt-injection mitigations [Source: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/, accessed 2 Oct 2026].

### 5.5 Data handling: the customer decides

- **Off until enabled.** Because the data is the customer's, Metis sends nothing to the third-party LLM until a tenant admin enables it on the consent screen. In the sales-led flow the provider may pre-select "on"; the executive, as first tenant admin, still accepts it explicitly.
- **Consent screen states:** which provider processes the content and in which region; what is sent (the fragments needed, the questions and answers, never other tenants' data); that the provider does not train on customer data; the provider's retention; what Metis keeps; how to switch the AI off; the rule-based path as the alternative.
- **Masking is the customer's choice:** sensitive personal fields beyond names, titles and work email (for example salaries or private phone numbers in a capacity sheet) are masked before sending by default; the tenant admin can switch masking off or extend it to further categories.
- **Sub-processors:** the LLM provider and any speech or vision service join the published sub-processor list (BRD Section 17, data lifecycle).
- **Inputs kept by Metis:** uploaded files are the customer's documents in their own tenant storage, kept as the source behind provenance links under the tenant's retention policy, with an option to delete them after launch (provenance then keeps file name and quoted passage only).
- **Transparency:** the conversation always presents the agent as AI (the square "AI" avatar convention of the wireframes), and every record it proposed shows "proposed by AI, approved by [person]". Where the EU AI Act applies, Article 50(1) requires informing people that they are interacting with an AI system, from 2 August 2026 [Source: https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/, accessed 2 Oct 2026] [Unverified - confirm applicability to Metis with counsel].
- **Model changes:** the provider and model version are recorded per onboarding session; a new model or provider is used only after the three suites pass.
- **Provider name is not a secret:** the sub-processor list and the consent screen name it. What stays protected is listed in 5.1. The agent itself does not discuss its internals.

Decisions this section adds (recommendations):
- **Provider selection criteria:** contractual no-training, zero or short retention, regional processing options, a data processing agreement, model version pinning. Selection in Discovery.
- **What the audit keeps for onboarding AI calls:** metadata and redacted excerpts by default; full prompt and reply kept only for calls flagged as security events, for 90 days (proposed), visible to the tenant admin. This mirrors open question Q-12 of the main BRD for MCP calls.

### 5.6 The fixed reply to probing

"I can help with anything about your company's data in Metis, but I can't share how I am built or anything about the systems behind Metis. Shall we continue with [current step]?" Shown in the user's language; the same reply for every out-of-scope request, so probing learns nothing from variations.

## 6. Bring-your-own-AI path (approved 2 Oct 2026)

### 6.1 Who it is for

- Tenants that keep Metis's onboarding AI switched off (policy, compliance, procurement).
- Teams whose own AI already reaches their documents. An enterprise assistant connected to the company's file stores can find and read files the executive would never upload; that makes this path richer, not only a fallback.
- Anyone who prefers to work from the AI client they use every day.

### 6.2 How it works

1. **Enable:** the tenant admin switches on the setup tool group for MCP clients (off by default, Section 3.5); the tenant's client allowlist applies (MCP-20).
2. **Connect:** the executive or a delegate opens "Set up with your own AI" in Metis. The page extends the AI access page (MCP-15, wireframe 08-profile-ai-access): the endpoint, OAuth or an **onboarding token** limited to the setup tools and the Draft workspace, with a short expiry (proposed 7 days, never above the tenant maximum, MCP-20), and a test call.
3. **Ask:** the user pastes one short prompt into their AI client. The intelligence is served by Metis, not by the prompt: the first tool call, `get_setup_context`, returns the framing answers, the starting pack, the record schemas, the order of work, the rules (cite a source for every value, never invent, raise a question instead of guessing) and the session's open questions. Prompts therefore stay short, work in any language and change when Metis changes, without anyone editing what they pasted.
4. **Work:** the client's AI reads the user's files in the user's environment and calls the same setup tools as Metis's own agent; validation errors come back in words the AI can act on, so it corrects itself (Section 3.5).
5. **Watch:** the Metis tab shows the same live feed, draft screens, cards and X-ray as Section 2, for example "Your AI added 34 projects and raised 6 questions".
6. **Launch in Metis only:** the launch summary and the single approval happen in the application (Section 4.6). The client's AI can never launch, invite or grant roles (BR-35).

### 6.3 The prompt pack

Copy-ready prompts, in the user's language:

| Job | Prompt (English version) |
|---|---|
| Set up from documents | "Use the Metis tools to set up our company from these files. Start with get_setup_context and follow it." |
| Import a project list | "Add the projects in this file to our Metis setup, with their owners, dates, budgets and status." |
| Describe how we approve projects | "From this handbook, describe in Metis how our projects get approved and who approves them." |
| Add our people | "Add the people in this org chart to our Metis setup with their titles and suggested roles." |
| Fill in budgets | "Fill in the budgets of our Metis projects from this finance sheet." |
| Answer open questions | "Get the open Metis setup questions and answer the ones these files can answer by proposing the values with the setup tools; leave the others." |

- Release 1 ships the pack as copy-ready text on the page and in the guide; serving the same prompts as MCP prompts follows MCP-17 (P1 in the main BRD), so this path adds no new P0 dependency.
- A user who keeps the setup context can also ask freely ("Our PMO handbook is in the shared drive; read it and set up our approval flow").

### 6.4 Data, quality and safety on this path

- **Data:** files are read by the customer's AI in the customer's environment; Metis receives only the proposals and the quoted sources. Metis's LLM provider is not involved; the customer's provider processes the data under the customer's own terms (BRD Section 17).
- **Provenance:** the client reports file name, location and quoted passage for each value; Metis stores them as "reported by your AI" and does not hold the file.
- **Quality:** Metis validation catches structural errors (an approval point without approvers, a missing stage), not wrong values; the same badges, cards and launch review apply. The verified-client list (MCP-15) gains a "verified for onboarding" mark for clients that pass Metis's onboarding test scenario.
- **Safety:** the guide advises running Metis setup without other connectors that can send data elsewhere (web, email) in the same session, following vendor guidance on prompt injection across MCP servers (`research/research-ai-onboarding.md` section 7.2); the boundary of Section 5 holds whatever the client does.
- **When IT blocks external MCP connections:** the rule-based path, or Metis's own onboarding AI if the tenant enables it (`research/research-ai-onboarding.md` section 4.3, Stripe's note that IT may block external MCP servers).

## 7. The addendum and its changes to the main BRD (approved 2 Oct 2026)

### 7.1 Form of the addendum

- A separate document, "BRD Addendum: Onboarding in 30 minutes", version 1.0, that supplements BRD v4.3 without editing it. Built like the main BRD: pandoc Markdown parts in `brd/source/addendum-onboarding/parts/`, generated `.md` and `.docx` in `brd/`, the same checks (IDs defined once, references resolved, no em dash, every P0 requirement on a wireframe).
- New module **M23 Onboarding & Data Intake**, requirement prefix **ONB**. Rules, decisions, questions and assumptions continue the main numbering (BR-43 onward, D-32 onward, Q-14 onward, A-08 onward) so no identifier collides.
- The main build learns the addendum's identifiers so the new wireframes can cite them and the P0 coverage check includes them; the main BRD text stays at v4.3 until a later release merges the addendum.
- Appendices: the option catalogue with its verdicts and the sourced market evidence, so the external review can check every claim.

### 7.3 New business rules (indicative wording)

| ID | Rule |
|---|---|
| BR-43 | The onboarding agent and MCP clients using the setup tool group write proposals only into a Draft workspace and its onboarding session; after launch they write suggestions that a person accepts. |
| BR-44 | Launch (publication, activation, invitations, role grants, adoption of projects) needs a person's approval in the application. |
| BR-45 | Every value created by onboarding keeps its source; a value without a source is shown as assumed or default until confirmed. |
| BR-46 | Stages completed before adoption are recorded with their sources and get no gate decision; exit rules (BR-17) apply from the adoption stage onward. |
| BR-47 | A baseline captured from imported values is labelled "from import" and changes only through change requests, like any baseline (BR-04, BR-05). |
| BR-48 | Auto-accept at a deadline keeps a value applied at launch; it never applies a new change. |
| BR-49 | Customer content goes to a third-party LLM only when the tenant has enabled it; it is never used for training; masking follows the tenant's settings. |
| BR-50 | No response on any channel reveals another tenant's data or existence, or Metis internals (database structure, hosts, keys, prompts); "not found" and "no access" are indistinguishable. |

### 7.6 Risks

| Risk | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong extraction paints a wrong portfolio | High | Sources on every value, badges, accuracy suite, launch review, undo window |
| Over-trust in baselines taken from documents | Medium | "From import" label; change requests as for any baseline |
| LLM provider outage, change or price rise | Medium | Rule-based path; model pinning; suites before any change; provider criteria |
| AI cost exceeds the price | Medium | Quotas, spend caps, exact parsers first |
| Personal data in uploaded documents | High | Consent, masking by default, sub-processor list, retention settings |
| Executives still drop off | High | Metrics per step; usability tests with design partners in the UX phase (BRD 18.4) |
| Owners ignore delegated tasks | Medium | Launch never waits; escalation; values kept by default with visible badges |
| Release 1 grows | Medium | Own workstream; milestone placement of 7.4; P1 options stay out of Release 1 |

## 9. Acceptance criteria and metrics (approved 2 Oct 2026)

### 9.1 Acceptance list

- From a tenant with pre-filled facts and a reference document set, an executive reaches the draft cockpit and then launches within the targets of 9.2, measured in moderated sessions with the design partners.
- The framing screen has three questions, none with a preset number, each skippable; the one-sentence answer sets the same values.
- Each supported input type is read; the kept-and-dropped report lists what was ignored and why; an MS Project or Project Online export becomes WBS items with dates and dependencies.
- Every value created by onboarding shows its source, or an "assumed" or "default" label.
- The executive sees no more cards than the cap; every other gap is assumed, defaulted, delegated or deferred and listed on the launch summary.
- In-flight projects are adopted at their current stage with history before Metis; committed ones get a baseline from import; no gate decision is fabricated.
- Approve and launch runs the seven steps in one transaction; a failing check blocks the launch and names its fix.
- Undo within the window removes the batch's records nobody changed and lists the others.
- Delegated tasks reach their owners; auto-accept keeps only values applied at launch; a suggestion after launch applies only when a person accepts it.
- A verified client sets up a Draft workspace from the prompt pack; launch happens only in Metis.
- With the onboarding AI switched off, the rule-based path sets up a workspace from structured files.
- The boundary, red-team and extraction-accuracy suites pass their criteria (Section 5.4).
- No customer content reaches the LLM provider before consent; masking is on by default.
- Every AI call, tool call, refusal and security event is in the tenant audit log.

### 9.2 Onboarding targets (proposed, to confirm with the design partners in Discovery)

| Measure | Proposed target |
|---|---|
| Executive hands-on time to the draft cockpit | 15 minutes or less (median) |
| Executive hands-on time to launch | 30 minutes or less (median) |
| Cards answered by the executive | 10 or fewer (median) |
| Values read with high confidence, assumed or defaulted, asked | Tracked; no target before the pilot |
| Values corrected within 14 days of launch | Tracked as the accuracy signal; target after the pilot |
| Delegated items closed by their due date | 80% or more |
| Onboarding sessions abandoned before launch | Tracked per step; target after the pilot |
| PM time to confirm their own adopted project | 5 minutes or less (median) |
| Days from launch to setup complete | Tracked |

### 9.3 Processing targets (proposed, to confirm with D-26 of the main BRD)

| Target | Proposed starting value |
|---|---|
| First card or first finding after the first file is dropped | Within 2 minutes |
| Draft cockpit ready for a reference set of about 20 documents | Within 10 minutes of the drop |
| Launch transaction | Within 1 minute for a reference portfolio of 50 projects and 100 people |
